summary: Defines the Dynamic Symmetric Key Provisioning Protocol, a client-server protocol for initializing symmetric keys in cryptographic modules, local or remote. It works with or without private key capabilities or a public key infrastructure.

plainLanguage.summary: A security token needs a secret number put into it. This protocol lets a server and a token agree on that number safely.

subtitle: How a security token or app gets its secret key from a provisioning server, either agreed jointly or delivered in protected form.

tldr.problem: Symmetric-key systems such as one-time passwords need a secret key placed in a cryptographic module. Keys were traditionally loaded at manufacture or shipped on a CD-ROM, and vendors often used proprietary, undocumented provisioning protocols.
tldr.mechanism: DSKPP is an XML client-server protocol carried over HTTP. The user is authenticated with a one-time Authentication Code, then the module and server either agree on a key together (four-pass) or the server sends a protected, pre-generated key (two-pass).
tldr.outcome: It gives an open, interoperable way to initialize and configure symmetric keys on local or remote modules, with or without private key capabilities or a public key infrastructure.

facts.label: PBKDF2 iterations for K_AC
facts.value: at least 100,000 (1 for K_SHARED or passphrase cases)

today: RFC 6063 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 4758 and uses the key container from RFC 6030.

sections.title: What DSKPP Provisions
sections.content:
Symmetric-key systems, such as one-time passwords and challenge-response authentication, offer performance and operational advantages over public key schemes. They need a way to provision the keys, comparable to what CMP and CMC do in a public key infrastructure.

The Dynamic Symmetric Key Provisioning Protocol (DSKPP) is a client-server protocol between a cryptographic module (reached through the DSKPP Client) and a key provisioning server (the DSKPP Server). Its description builds on RFC 4758 (CT-KIP) and adds user authentication and support for the RFC 6030 key container format.

The protocol has two variants. The four-pass variant establishes a key containing randomness from both client and server. The two-pass variant needs only one round trip and establishes a key chosen by the server. Only version 1.0 is specified, and the version number exists so that algorithms and key sizes can change without disrupting existing implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret-number gadget cannot do its job until someone puts a secret number inside it. DSKPP is the safe way to do that over the internet.

sections.title: Entities and Authentication
sections.content:
A provisioning run has three entities: the server, the cryptographic module that will receive the key (for example an authentication token), and the client that manages communication between them. The messages are XML layered on HTTP, ideally over TLS. The RFC stresses that TLS alone is not enough to protect the key exchange, so DSKPP is built to protect the key data itself.

The server MUST authenticate the user before issuing a key. There are two ways. In the first, the client starts the protocol and the user is authenticated inside it with a Client ID and an Authentication Code (AC) delivered out of band, such as a paper slip. These are often short numeric values, for example 8 decimal digits. In the second, the user first signs in to a web application, which replies with a <KeyProvTrigger> message carrying the Client ID, Authentication Code and server URL; the browser hands it to the DSKPP Client.

The AC is encoded as type-length-value triples: Client ID (type 1) and Password (type 2) are mandatory, and a Checksum (type 3) computed with CRC16 is optional. The Authentication Data (AD) sent on the wire is a MAC derived from the AC using DSKPP-PRF, with the key K_AC derived by PBKDF2. The iteration count MUST be at least 100,000, except for two two-pass cases where it MUST be 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the gadget gets its secret, the owner proves who they are with a one-time code, like a ticket handed over in person. The code is only used once.

sections.title: Choosing a Variant
sections.content:
Both variants start with the client sending a <KeyProvClientHello> that includes a Security Attribute List (SAL): the versions, variants, key package formats, key types and algorithms it supports, favorite first. The server picks an acceptable combination or returns a failure status.

The four-pass variant is needed when policy requires both parties to contribute entropy, when the module has no private key capabilities, or when the device has neither a manufacturer's key or other pre-shared key nor a keypad for entering a passphrase.

The two-pass variant is needed when pre-existing (legacy) keys must be transported to the module, when the device was pre-issued with a manufacturer's key or other pre-shared key and can do private key operations, or when it has a keypad for entering a passphrase.

On any status other than Success or Continue, both sides MUST end the run and delete any secret values generated. The RFC defines many status codes, including AccessDenied, AuthenticationDataInvalid, NoSupportedKeyTypes, UnsupportedVersion and ProvisioningPeriodExpired.
sections.plainLanguage: The gadget and the server first agree on which set of rules to use, like picking a game that both players know. Then they play it.

sections.title: The Four-Pass Exchange
sections.content:
In four-pass DSKPP the key is generated on the fly and never sent over the wire. Two exchanges happen. Pass 1 and 2 (<KeyProvClientHello> and <KeyProvServerHello>) negotiate algorithms and give the client the server's random nonce R_S and a key K, which is either the server's public key (K_SERVER) or a pre-shared key (K_SHARED). If an existing key is being renewed, the server also sends a MAC so the client can confirm the replacement comes from a trusted server.

Pass 3 (<KeyProvClientNonce>) carries the client's own random nonce R_C encrypted under K, plus the Authentication Data. The server authenticates the user, decrypts R_C, and both sides compute the provisioning key: K_PROV = DSKPP-PRF(R_C, "Key generation" || K || R_S, dsLen). Its first half is K_MAC and its second half is K_TOKEN.

Pass 4 (<KeyProvServerFinished>) holds a key package with the key ID and usage attributes but not the key itself, plus a key confirmation MAC. With status Success it acts as a commit: the client verifies the MAC, derives K_TOKEN and stores it. Afterwards the key cannot be overwritten unless the sender proves knowledge of an authorizing key through a MAC.

Because both nonces and K feed the key, each side knows it contributed to the key's randomness. A man in the middle who substitutes his own public key ends up with a K_TOKEN that does not match the legitimate server's.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side thinks of a secret number and mixes it with the other's. Neither ever says the final number out loud, yet both end up with the same one.

sections.title: The Two-Pass Exchange and Key Protection
sections.content:
Two-pass DSKPP is essentially a transport of keying material from server to client in one round trip. The client's <KeyProvClientHello> carries the SAL, its Authentication Data, a nonce R and a list of supported key protection methods (the KPML). The server generates K_PROV = K_MAC || K_TOKEN by itself, encrypts it with one of the client's methods, and returns it in a key package in <KeyProvServerFinished>, along with a key confirmation MAC.

Three key protection methods are defined:

  • Key Transport, for PKI-capable devices: the server encrypts with the client's public key.
  • Key Wrap, for pre-keyed devices such as SIM cards: the server uses a pre-shared key wrapping key.
  • Passphrase-Based Key Wrap, for constrained devices with keypads: the wrapping key comes from a user-provided passphrase using PBKDF2.

When an existing key is being replaced, the server also sends a second MAC (the server authentication MAC) in the AD field so the client can confirm the sender is trusted. The default key package format MUST be based on the Portable Symmetric Key Container from RFC 6030; alternatives MAY include RFC 6031, PKCS #12 or PKCS #5 XML.

One worked example in the RFC: for an HOTP key of length 20 with DSKPP-PRF-SHA256, K_PROV is 64 bytes, K_TOKEN and K_MAC are 32 bytes each, and the HOTP key is the first 20 bytes of K_TOKEN.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the server picks the secret itself and puts it in a locked box. Only the gadget has the key to the box, so the secret travels safely.

sections.title: Extensions, HTTP Binding and Schema
sections.content:
DSKPP messages are XML in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:keyprov:dskpp, and UTF-8 is the only allowed encoding. Messages can carry extensions; an extension marked Critical that a receiver cannot interpret causes the UnknownCriticalExtension status. Two are defined: ClientInfoType and ServerInfoType, opaque data that the other side must echo back unchanged in its next message.

DSKPP assumes a reliable transport, and the HTTP/1.1 binding is mandatory to implement. All messages use the MIME type application/dskpp+xml. Requests are HTTP POSTs, and responses use status 200 whenever the POST succeeded, even if the DSKPP message carries an error. A server refusing an exchange SHOULD return 403, an internal HTTP-level error is a 500, and a request that is not a DSKPP client message gets a 400. Caching is discouraged with no-cache style headers. In four-pass runs the SessionID in the server hello binds the later client nonce message to the same run.

Section 8 gives the full XML schema, and the appendices give usage scenarios, example messages, a PKCS #11 integration and the two DSKPP-PRF realizations, DSKPP-PRF-AES and DSKPP-PRF-SHA256.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are written in a tidy, labeled format and delivered by the same carrier that delivers web pages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DSKPP is designed so that only the server and the cryptographic module ever have K_TOKEN, even if malicious software is present in the client, provided the algorithms are strong and the module generates R_C and K_TOKEN as specified. It does not defend against every man-in-the-middle threat, so it MUST be run over a transport giving confidentiality and integrity, such as HTTP over TLS, when those threats matter. TLS cipher suites with anonymous key exchange are not suitable.

The RFC walks through active attacks. Modified hellos could downgrade algorithms or versions, so implementations may enforce strict policies. Deleted messages only cause denial of service, because the module does not commit until it validates the final message's MAC. Replay and reordering are detected through the nonces and unique message types. A captured trigger message lets an eavesdropper race the user, so the trigger needs a protected transport.

Servers should not bind a new K_TOKEN to a user until the user proves both possession of the device and out-of-band information. In two-pass DSKPP only the server adds entropy, so a weak server random number generator does more damage; servers should take extreme care. Passphrase-based wrapping is limited in strength, so the RFC lists extra measures such as per-key random passphrases and high PBKDF2 counts.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys might try to trick the gadget or listen in. The protocol uses one-time codes, fresh random numbers and checks at the end so a trick leaves the gadget unchanged.

messages.note: SAL, AD, R_C, KPML, optional DeviceID and KeyID.
